sentence: Grief is a normal response to loss, and the NHS says feelings of sadness should ease gradually over time.
NHS Inform says there is no time limit on grief.
The NHS says to see a GP if someone is struggling to cope, or their own efforts are not helping.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.
Grief can bring shock, numbness, sadness, exhaustion and anger.
NHS Inform says there is no time limit on grief and advises against rushing back to usual responsibilities.
Delayed grief can be triggered by a later loss, and it is never too late to grieve.
An NHS trust lists shock and numbness, overwhelming sadness, tiredness or exhaustion, anger and guilt among common reactions.

sentence: The NHS suggests talking to a friend, family member or counsellor, regular exercise and regular meals.
It advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to ease grief, because these can worsen mental health.
Bereavement support organisations such as Cruse can help, and talking to others can bring comfort.
The NHS says sadness should ease gradually with time, but medical help may be needed if someone feels increasingly depressed or anxious.
It advises seeing a GP when someone is struggling to cope, has had low mood for more than two weeks, or finds their own efforts are not helping.
A GP surgery can refer someone to a therapist or counsellor.
The NHS has a bereavement hub, with a section on children and bereavement as well as grief after a bereavement or loss.
Cruse Bereavement Support offers a helpline and information on dealing with grief, and Child Bereavement UK and Winston's Wish support bereaved children and families.

sentence: For some people grief does not lessen even after a long time, and the NHS notes this may be a mental health condition called prolonged grief disorder.
Signs the NHS lists include difficulty accepting the death and suicidal thoughts, and it advises seeing a GP with these.
If grief brings thoughts of not wanting to go on, urgent help is available. NHS inform in Scotland points to NHS 24 on 111.

sentence: If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E.
note: Trust pages: if life is at risk, someone is in immediate danger or has harmed themselves, call 999 or go to A&E.

sentence: For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf.
note: NHS trust page: call NHS 111 option 2 for urgent mental health support; 24/7; can call for yourself or someone else.

sentence: Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.
note: Samaritans 116 123 free, 24 hours: returned in the urgent-help and NHS grief searches.
